title: Aqueducts
objective: After this level you can explain how aqueducts carried water to Roman cities using gravity.
summary: Aqueducts ran on a gentle downhill slope, mostly underground. By the 3rd century CE, 11 of them fed the city of Rome.

cards.headline: Rome brought water into the city without a single pump.
cards.body: No engines, no waterwheels. Just one force that never takes a day off.

cards.headline: Downhill all the way
cards.body: An aqueduct was a very long, very gentle slide. Water flowed by gravity along a steady downhill slope from springs in the hills. And the famous arches? They’re the exception. Most of an aqueduct’s length ran underground or at ground level. Arches only carried it across valleys, where the ground dropped away but the slope had to stay steady. Keep the slope steady, and the water keeps coming.

mascot.line: People picture the arches. But most of an aqueduct ran underground or at ground level.

cards.headline: Water for a city
cards.body: Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, was built in 312 BCE by Appius Claudius, the same man who began the Appian Way. Roads and water in the same year: busy man. More followed, and by the 3rd century CE, 11 aqueducts supplied the city. Water mattered so much that Rome had a water commissioner. Around 97 CE that was Frontinus, who wrote a whole book about the aqueducts.

cards.fact: The Pont du Gard still stands in southern France.
cards.context: It’s one of those valley-crossing bridges: three tiers of arches, about 49 m high, all to keep the water on its gentle downhill slope.

cards.headline: Water: delivered
learned: Most of their length was hidden
Rome’s first was built in 312 BCE

questions.prompt: What moved water through a Roman aqueduct?
questions.explanation: Aqueducts ran on a gentle, steady downhill slope, so gravity did the work.

questions.prompt: Why did aqueducts need arches in some places?

options.label: To show off the emperor’s wealth
To keep the slope steady across valleys
To hold up the city walls

questions.explanation: Arches carried the channel across dips in the land, keeping the gentle slope unbroken.

questions.prompt: From Level 19: Appius Claudius built Rome’s first aqueduct. What else did he begin?
questions.explanation: Appius Claudius began both the Aqua Appia and the Via Appia in 312 BCE.
